query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: When a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially prepared as a homogeneous, metastable solid solution is subjected to controlled heat treatment simulating service conditions, the thermal activation triggers diffusion-driven nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates deplete the matrix of the elements needed for a continuous protective oxide scale, thereby compromising the alloy’s corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state with a uniform elemental distribution and an intact, continuous passivating oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Controlled heat treatment at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., above approximately 600°C) for durations sufficient for significant atomic diffusion.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature oxidative and/or corrosive environments in a regime where diffusion and intermetallic nucleation become thermally activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates formed by diffusion-driven local compositional clustering.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated atomic diffusion leads to local enrichment of Mg that initiates the nucleation of intermetallic compounds. As these precipitates grow and coarsen, they disrupt the continuity and distribution of the protective oxide scale that was present in the as-cast metastable state, ultimately reducing the material’s corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated metastable state, heat-treated samples will exhibit a measurable increase in the formation and coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallic phases along grain boundaries and within the matrix, accompanied by a statistically significant deterioration in corrosion resistance and higher oxidation mass gains.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, homogeneous metastable solid-solution alloy that displays a continuous, intact passivating oxide layer and correspondingly robust corrosion/oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: The transformation is expected to become significant under service conditions in which the temperature and exposure time exceed the kinetic thresholds for Mg diffusion and intermetallic nucleation (e.g., sustained exposures above ~600°C).
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of intermetallic nucleation and the critical temperature/duration thresholds may vary with alloy composition, and further quantification is needed to define precise parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA specimens: one set is preserved in the as-cast metastable state (via rapid quenching) while the other set is subjected to controlled heat treatment at temperatures above 600°C for extended durations. Perform microstructural characterization using TEM, SEM, and XRD to quantify the presence, size, and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Concurrently, assess corrosion resistance using standardized electrochemical tests and evaluate oxidation behavior through thermogravimetric measurements.
measurements: TEM/SEM imaging and elemental mapping to quantify precipitate formation
XRD for phase identification and quantification of intermetallic compounds
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization for corrosion resistance
Oxidation weight gain measurements over time at designated high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the formation or coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the as-cast control, or if the corrosion and oxidation resistances remain statistically indistinguishable from those of the as-cast state under identical service conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

The nanocrystalline FexCrNiAl (x = 1.0, 0.5, 0.25) high-entropy alloy powders with supersaturated BCC phases were synthesized by mechanical alloying successfully. The alloying behavior, morphology, and phase evolution of the powders were discussed systematically. The continuous collision of high-energy milling facilitated the diffusion and dissolution of each component; the alloyed powders have a crystalline size of ~80 nm, resulting in a high dislocation density of ~1015 m−2, which lowered the subsequent sintering temperature. And the powders particles have excellent homogeneity in composition with a mean particle size of 1.59~1.82 μm. The non-equilibrium supersaturated solid solution phase transformed into the equilibrium phase of BCC and ordered BCC (B2) phases after annealing at temperatures from 800 °C to 1000 °C, and the volume fraction of the B2 phase increased with the annealing temperature, reaching about 49.44% at 1000 °C.

Magnesium-containing multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are promising for lightweight applications due to their low density, high specific strength, and biocompatibility. This study examines two Mg-Ti-Zn alloy compositions, equal molar MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ), synthesized via ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, focusing on their microstructures and corrosion behaviors. X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy revealed the formation of intermetallic phases, including Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25 in TZ, while 4TZ exhibited a predominantly Mg-rich phase. Potentiodynamic polarization and immersion tests in 0.1 M NaCl solution showed that both alloys had good corrosion resistance, with values of 3.65 ± 0.65 µA/cm2 for TZ and 4.58 ± 1.64 µA/cm2 for 4TZ. This was attributed to the formation of a TiO2-rich surface film in the TZ, as confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), which contributed to enhanced passivation and lower corrosion current density. drafts.hypothesis: High-temperature exposure of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy promotes a phase separation that nucleates intermetallic compounds at Mg-rich sites; this precipitation concurrently depletes the matrix of protective elements, leading to a transformation of the microstructure that correlates with a loss (or weakening) of corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable solid‐solution state with a relatively homogeneous distribution of Mg and other alloying elements.
drafts.intervention: A controlled heat treatment (annealing) at service-relevant temperatures designed to simulate prolonged high-temperature exposure.
drafts.conditions: A direct comparison between specimens preserved in the as-quenched state and those annealed at temperatures typical of the intended service regime (e.g., above ~600°C) for varying durations (e.g., 10–100 hours).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of intermetallic compound precipitates, particularly at grain boundaries or local regions where Mg becomes enriched.
drafts.mechanism: Upon annealing, diffusion kinetics enable the segregation of Mg and other species into discrete intermetallic phases. This nucleation and growth process depletes the residual matrix of components that initially contributed to corrosion and oxidation resistance, thereby altering the microstructural stability and degrading the protective properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit a significant emergence of intermetallic precipitates (verified via TEM/SEM and compositional mapping) along with a measurable reduction in corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance compared to the as-quenched state.
drafts.baseline: The as-quenched, homogeneous metastable solid-solution state, which demonstrates initially robust corrosion and oxidation resistance.
drafts.boundary: The effect is expected to become pronounced when service conditions exceed a thermal-activation threshold (approximately >600°C for sufficient duration) that enables rapid diffusion and phase separation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens: one set remains in the as-quenched state, and the other is annealed under specified service-relevant conditions. Employ microstructural characterization (TEM, SEM, EDS) and measure electrochemical corrosion rates and high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
measurements: Identification and quantification of intermetallic precipitates (e.g., precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction)
Elemental mapping to assess depletion of protective components in the matrix
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show significant intermetallic compound formation compared to the as-quenched control, or if there is no concurrent decrease in corrosion/oxidation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: When exposed to service conditions (moderate to high temperatures in oxidative or corrosive environments), the initially metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution in a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy undergoes a decomposition via Mg enrichment and local spinodal-like clustering that nucleates Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates. This transformation creates microstructural heterogeneities that initially may sustain a protective oxide through fine-scale dispersion, but as intermetallic particles coarsen and local composition gradients grow, the continuity of the passivating oxide is disrupted, resulting in a measured loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Metastable, non-equilibrium high-entropy alloy in a solid-solution state with uniform composition
drafts.intervention: Controlled heat treatment that mimics service conditions (e.g., sustained exposure to temperatures above a critical threshold) to stimulate phase decomposition
drafts.conditions: Service-regime boundaries characterized by temperatures and exposure times sufficient to drive Mg diffusion and intermetallic nucleation (e.g., temperatures typically >600 °C for durations on the scale of hours) under oxidative or corrosive environments
drafts.structural_mediator: Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form via local compositional clustering from the solid-solution state
drafts.mechanism: Kinetic spinodal-like decomposition leads to Mg clustering that nucleates intermetallic phases. Initially, fine dispersion of these phases might be compatible with protective oxide scale formation; however, as the precipitates coarsen and disrupt the continuity of the oxide, corrosion and oxidation resistance deteriorate.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, metastable state, heat-treated samples will show the emergence and growth of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic phases (evident by TEM/XRD) and a subsequent reduction in the integrity of the passivating oxide, leading to accelerated corrosion rates and higher oxidation mass gains.
drafts.baseline: The untreated metastable solid-solution alloy exhibiting near-uniform composition and high inherent corrosion/oxidation resistance due to continuous and uniform oxide passivation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies when service conditions exceed the kinetic and thermal thresholds for Mg diffusion and intermetallic nucleation (e.g., temperatures >600 °C for extended periods), beyond which the microstructural evolution disrupts oxide continuity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing high-entropy alloy samples: one group maintained in the as-cast metastable state and the other subjected to a controlled heat treatment mimicking service conditions (e.g., >600 °C for several hours). Analyze both groups using microstructural characterization methods (TEM, SEM, XRD) for the presence and evolution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and assess corrosion/oxidation behavior using standardized electrochemical and thermogravimetric tests.
measurements: Phase identification and distribution via TEM and XRD
Precipitate size and spatial distribution via SEM
Corrosion rates using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy/potentiodynamic polarization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show significant formation or growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the as-cast baseline, or if corrosion/oxidation resistance remains statistically indistinguishable between treated and untreated samples under the tested conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the initial non-equilibrium metastable solid-solution state evolves during service via a diffusion-driven nucleation process that produces nanoscale intermetallic precipitates (especially along grain boundaries). This precipitation depletes the alloy of key elements required for forming protective oxide scales, thereby reducing the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast state. Conversely, samples with minimized intermetallic formation (through controlled thermal exposure) will sustain better corrosion and oxidation performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a metastable solid-solution-containing state
drafts.intervention: Subject samples to controlled heat treatment or service-simulated thermal exposure versus an untreated control
drafts.conditions: High-temperature oxidation (600–900 °C) and corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution)
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates especially nucleated at grain boundaries
drafts.mechanism: Diffusion-driven nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds deplete alloying elements that otherwise form continuous, protective oxide films. The loss of these elements reduces the formation and stability of protective scales, thereby impairing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples that develop extensive intermetallic precipitation will exhibit higher oxidation weight gains and increased corrosion current density relative to the as-cast, metastable state, while those with minimal precipitate formation retain enhanced protective behavior.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium metastable solid-solution state with limited intermetallic content and inherent protective oxide formation ability
drafts.boundary: Service regimes characterized by temperatures and exposure durations where diffusional transformations become significant, for example, long-duration exposures at 600–900 °C or prolonged immersion in chloride-containing environments

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to controlled heat treatments designed to promote intermetallic precipitation (e.g., prolonged exposure at 800 °C) while retaining the other set in the as-cast metastable state. Characterize both sets using TEM and X-ray diffraction to assess intermetallic formation. Test high-temperature oxidation resistance (via oxidation weight gain measurements) and corrosion resistance (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
measurements: Oxidation kinetics (weight gain vs. time) at designated temperatures
Corrosion current densities and impedance spectra in NaCl solution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with extensive intermetallic precipitation do not show a statistically significant degradation in oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to the untreated metastable state, then the hypothesis that intermetallic precipitation compromises protective oxide formation is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In the Mg-containing lightweight HEA, the non‐equilibrium solid solution evolves through thermally activated, diffusion‐mediated nucleation of intermetallic compounds at defect sites, which in turn governs the formation and integrity of protective oxide films. When these intermetallic precipitates form and coarsen, they disrupt the uniform passivation established in the metastable state, thereby reducing high‐temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium single-phase solid solution containing Mg along with other alloying elements (e.g., Ti and Zn) exhibiting high lattice distortion and a high defect density.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled heat treatment (or aging) regime that enables diffusion and transformation of the metastable state.
drafts.conditions: Service-relevant high temperatures (approximately 500–1000 °C) and corrosive environments (such as exposure to air for oxidation and 3.5 wt.% NaCl solutions for corrosion) over extended durations.
drafts.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds (for example, phases akin to Ti2Zn or Mg21Zn25) that mediate local compositional partitioning and influence the adherence and continuity of resulting oxide films (e.g., formation of TiO2-rich layers).
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation enhances atomic diffusion, causing solute redistribution and local segregation at defects (such as grain boundaries and dislocations). These sites act as nucleation points for intermetallic phases. As these precipitates evolve (either remaining finely dispersed or coarsening), they alter the nucleation kinetics and growth morphology of protective oxide layers. A uniform, fine dispersion may help sustain a continuous passivating film, while coarsening leads to discontinuities that lower corrosion and oxidation resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous metastable state, samples that exhibit significant intermetallic compound precipitation will show modified oxidation and corrosion behavior: if intermetallics coarsen, the protective oxide film will become less uniform and more permeable, resulting in increased oxidation weight gain and higher corrosion current densities. Conversely, if precipitates remain finely distributed, some protective effects may be retained.
drafts.baseline: The initial metastable solid solution state is expected to have a uniform microstructure with a homogeneous passivation layer, yielding optimal corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.boundary: The transformation pathway and its impact are expected to be most significant when service temperatures exceed ~500 °C over prolonged exposure durations, where diffusion becomes appreciable; these conditions also define the regime where rapid versus gradual intermetallic evolution can critically alter the protective oxide formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing HEA samples: one maintained in the as-cast metastable state (via rapid quenching) and the other subjected to a controlled heat treatment to promote intermetallic compound formation. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., in air at ~900 °C) and corrosion testing (e.g., immersion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under identical conditions for extended periods.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to quantify intermetallic precipitate formation and assess microstructural evolution
Oxidation weight gain measurements and analysis of oxide scale morphology via electron microscopy
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization to evaluate corrosion resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the volume fraction and coarsening of intermetallic phases compared to the metastable state – or if the predicted degradation in oxide scale integrity and corresponding increases in oxidation/corrosion rates are not observed – then the hypothesis is falsified.
